title: Homework 4 - Visual Solutions
text:
This assignment is intended to give you experience with linear regression. You won’t need to bring in your own datasets—everything you need comes from R packages. Homework datasets and solutions are included in the stat1080r course package, so make sure you have the latest version installed before you begin.
You’ll complete this file by finishing the code and filling in the answer prompts. Replace each #...# with the code needed to answer the question. Sometimes I’ll give you a code “shell” (marked with ##) that you’ll need to uncomment and complete.
When you’re done, submit your .qmd file in Canvas. Be sure it successfully renders to HTML with all your answers showing. Also remember to run lintr on your assignment so that you don’t lose points for style.
There are 3 problems in this assignment (each with several parts), worth a total of 56 points. Don’t forget to check the style guidelines at the end before submitting. Note that you must use the “modern” pipe command |> in your code. Please avoid the use of the old %>% in your code which will result in a loss of points.

title: Homework 4 - Visual Solutions
text:
Part a (2 points)
Before we try creating any regression models, lets first make sure that a linear model is an appropriate way to represent the data. First, remove all rows that have missing values for square footage or price. Second, modify the price variable to be in thousands of dollars (it is currently given in dollars).

title: Homework 4 - Visual Solutions
text:
Part b (5 points)
Next, create a density plot that looks at the distribution of house prices and a density plot that looks at the distribution of house square footage. Both plots will include three density curves, one for each subdivision.
The following code chunk creates three separate plot themes. One theme places the legend in the upper right corner, one theme places it in the upper left corner, and one theme removes it entirely. You will need to choose between these themes to help you format your plots to look exactly like the provided solution.
In addition to using the provided plot themes, you will also need to change the x and y axis labels, titles, and limits to match the provided solution plot (see homework_4_visual_sol.html). You will also need to use the Dark2 color pallet using the scale_color_brewer() function.






Density plots of house prices and square footage in Mount Pleasant, South Carolina.

title: Homework 4 - Visual Solutions
text:
Part c (3 points)
Write a few sentences interpreting the plots. Be sure to address which neighborhoods, if any, seem to have house prices or house square footage that follow a normal distribution. Also address whether or not you think the prices and/or square footage distributions are similar across neighborhoods.


Answer: The distribution of house prices and square footage are NOT the same when comparing the three neighborhoods. The Carolina park neighborhood has a much smaller range of typical house prices and sizes, making me think it is a highly planned neighborhood with “cookie cutter” houses. Prices and square footage in Dunes West and Park West are very right skewed. Carolina Park seems to have prices and square footage values that are closest to following a normal distribution, but there seems to be MORE values near the average (i.e. shorter tails) than we would expect if the data followed a normal distribution.

title: Homework 4 - Visual Solutions
text:
Part d (2 points)
Linear regression works better when the variables we use in our model are not skewed (though they don’t have to necessarily be normally distributed). Because of this, we are going to see if square footage shares a linear relationship with house price when looking at the natural log-transformation (i.e. log() in R) of both variables. Keeping this in mind, create two new variables that represent the log-transformation of house price and square footage and add them to the dataset. Call these variables log_price and log_sqft respectively.

title: Homework 4 - Visual Solutions
text:
Part e (3 points)
Now, use the log-transformed variables to make a scatterplot that relates the log-transformed square footage to the log-transformed prices. Do not distinguish the points by neighborhood in this plot. Use the same format and style considerations outlined in Part b to get your version of this plot to match the solution plot exactly.






Scatterplot relating square footage to house price.

title: Homework 4 - Visual Solutions
text:
Part f (2 points)
Based on this plot, do you think it is appropriate to try and create a linear model that uses square footage to predict house price? Explain why or why not.


Answer: I would say that the data do seem to share a linear relationship (i.e. we could fit a straight line through the center of the points). Because of this, it seems appropriate to use linear regression to relate square footage and house price.

title: Homework 4 - Visual Solutions
text:
Part g (3 points)
Using a similar plot style to Part e and an identical color scheme to Part f, plot the points using color to distinguish subdivisions. Use the geom_smooth(method = "lm") argument to look at estimated regression lines for each neighborhood.






Scatterplot relating square footage to house price by subdivision.

title: Homework 4 - Visual Solutions
text:
Part h (3 points)
Based on those regression line and their associated confidence intervals (i.e., the gray shaded regions), does it visually appear at the relationship between house price and square footage is the same across all subdivisions? Explain why or why not (using visuals only, no statistical tests at this point).


Answer: The relationship appears to be identical for the Dunes West and Park West subdivisions, but very different for the Carolina Park Subdivision. Carolina Park house prices seem to be less responsive to changes in square footage than the other two neighborhoods.

Use the housing dataset that removed the missing price and square footage values and includes the log-transformed price and square footage variables. Create a simple linear regression model using the lm() function that uses the log-transformed square footage to predict the log-transformed price.

title: Homework 4 - Visual Solutions
text:
Part b (3 points)
Use the predict() function with your newly created linear model to predict house prices from 1000 sqft to 3000 sqft in increments of 100. Remember that your predictions will be on the log scale, so you will need to use the exp() function to transform your predictions back to the original scale.

title: Homework 4 - Visual Solutions
text:
Part c (2 points)
Lets now consider a model that includes both square footage and lot size (i.e. acres) as predictors. To do this, we will first need to create a log-transformed version of acres, i.e. log(acres + 0.1). The + 0.1 accommodates the fact that some of the homes have no lot since they are condos, and you cannot take the log of zero.
Add log_acres to your housing dataset and make sure that the new dataset matches the solution exactly.

title: Homework 4 - Visual Solutions
text:
Part d (3 points)
Use the lm() function to create a linear model that uses log_acres and log_sqft to predict log_price. Confirm that your linear model matches the solution exactly.

title: Homework 4 - Visual Solutions
text:
Part e (5 points)
Use the confint() function to obtain 95% confidence intervals for all of the model coefficients. We wish to use the confidence intervals to determine if, after accounting for the square footage of the home, lot size is still significantly related to house price. Based on your confidence intervals, what do you conclude and why?


Answer: There is significant evidence to suggest that, after accounting for home square footage, that lot size is linearly related to house price. We can say this because the chance that there is no relationship (i.e. a coefficient the log_acres term equal to 0) is very small based on our sample because our confidence interval does not include zero.

title: Homework 4 - Visual Solutions
text:
Part a (5 points)
Use the tidy() function from the broom package to create a dataframe of coefficients (with associated confidence intervals) for three linear models, one for each subdivision, that use log_sqft and log_acres to predict log_price. Remember to use a group_by() operation on an appropriate variable in order to get the tidy() function to give you coefficients for three models instead of one.

title: Homework 4 - Visual Solutions
text:
Part b (5 points)
Use geom_segment() and facet_wrap() to plot the confidence intervals for the coefficients associated with log_sqft and log_acres. Most of the code is provided, but you need to figure out how to complete the statement for the geom_segment() function. Please consult the function documentation to do this. The result of this code is separate plots for the two variables, with subdivisions provided on the y-axis and the confidence intervals plotted on the x-axis (see the solution plot).






Plots of the confidence intervals associated with the subdivision-specific linear model coefficient estimates.

title: Homework 4 - Visual Solutions
text:
Part c (3 points)
Interpret the results of Part a and b in a few sentences. Do the estimated coefficients appear to be roughly similar to the overall model results? Does your conclusions regarding the statistical significance (or lack thereof) in Problem 2, Part e fail to hold in any of the subdivision-specific models?


Answer: Home prices in Carolina Park seem to be much less responsive to house size as compared to the other two subdivisions. I say this because there is literally no overlap in the confidence intervals associated with coefficient estimates for log_sqft. The other two subdivisions seem to be similar in all respects, and the coefficient estimates associated with lot size seem to be roughly similar (as evidenced by confidence interval overlap) in all subdivisions.

Can’t We Fix This With Better Phrasing?
Samuel J. Gershman and Tomer D. Ullman “Causal Implicatures from Correlational Statements,” PLOS ONE 18, no. 5 (May 18, 2023): e0286067, https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0286067.

People infer causation from correlational statements, using the variable order as a directional indicator

Even with “X is associated with an increased risk of Y” language
Even when given the choice of non-causal interpretations, 47% of people still use causal interpretations



In summary, certain correlational statements are associated with an increased probability of causal implicature. To be clear, we are not implying that these correlational statements cause causal implicature, but rather that they are correlated with causal implicature. In other words, correlation does not imply causation, but it does sometimes “imply” causation.

Be suspicious if


There aren’t many data points and/or data points have been cherry-picked in some way
There are a large number of possible variables to compare

Example: 2008 Recession Economic Policy
Economists Reinhart and Rogoff published a paper, Growth in a Time of Debt (2010), arguing:

median growth rates for countries with public debt over 90 percent of GDP are roughly one percent lower than otherwise; average (mean) growth rates are several percent lower.

Issues:

Years of high debt and average growth were selectively excluded from the data set
Countries’ GDP growth rates were not properly weighted
Summary table excludes high-debt and average-growth countries

Motivation
I want to explore the links between caffeine intake, heart rate, and length of sleep over the course of the semester. Caffeine does not make me more alert (it makes me sleepy, it’s an ADHD thing) but physiologically there is no reason to expect that it would not increase my heart rate.
I expect that on days that I am more active (as measured by maximum heart rate and steps), I need more sleep to recover. I am interested in discovering whether my caffeine intake changes on those days, and whether there appears to be any relationship between caffeine and maximum heart rate or caffeine and sleep length.


Methodology
Sleep will be tracked using Sleep as Droid, which requires manually starting a sleep session. The data is saved on a separate Google calendar as well as shared with Google Fit. Sleep session data is stored as a JSON file, but the duration is a top-level value and can be exported relatively easily. Alternately, the app logs can be used to manually type duration information into a spreadsheet, which can be exported to CSV.
Any data not exported from Google Fit automatically will be filled in using the calendar sync.
Caffeine data will be tracked manually in a spreadsheet between September 9 and November 11 (a total of 9 weeks). Caffeine on packaged drinks will be logged according to the nutritional information; black tea will be logged as 70 mg per 8 oz (the high end of the typical estimate) as it is difficult to measure caffeine content exactly in loose-leaf tea. The spreadsheet data will be exported to a CSV at the end of data collection.
Data from the different sources will be merged together by date using tidyr’s join functions.

    legend.position = "inside",
    legend.position.inside = c(1, 1),
    legend.justification.inside = c(1, 1),
    legend.background = element_blank(),
    text = element_text(size = 16)
  )

# Use the following theme to get the legend in the upper left corner
theme_legend_left <- theme_bw() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "inside",
    legend.position.inside = c(0, 1),
    legend.justification.inside = c(0, 1),
    legend.background = element_blank(),
    text = element_text(size = 16)
  )

# Use the following theme to get rid of the legend
theme_no_legend <- theme_bw() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "none",
    text = element_text(size = 16)
  )

p1 <- ggplot(housing, aes(x = price, color = subdivision)) +
  geom_density(lwd = 1) +
  scale_x_continuous("Price (thousands of dollars)",
    limits = c(0, 2000)
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous("", limits = c(0, .006)) +
  scale_color_brewer(type = "qual", palette = "Dark2") +

  geom_density(lwd = 1) +
  scale_x_continuous("Square Footage",
    limits = c(500, 8000),
    breaks = seq(500, 8000, 1500)

title: Homework 4 - STAT 1080
text:
Part c (3 points)
Write a few sentences interpreting the plots. Be sure to address which neighborhoods, if any, seem to have house prices or house square footage that follow a normal distribution. Also address whether or not you think the prices and/or square footage distributions are similar across neighborhoods.


Answer: The distribution of house prices and square footage are NOT the same when comparing the three neighborhoods. The Carolina park neighborhood has a much smaller range of typical house prices and sizes, making me think it is a highly planned neighborhood with “cookie cutter” houses. Prices and square footage in Dunes West and Park West are very right skewed. Carolina Park seems to have prices and square footage values that are closest to following a normal distribution, but there seems to be MORE values near the average (i.e. shorter tails) than we would expect if the data followed a normal distribution.

title: Homework 4 - STAT 1080
text:
Part d (2 points)
Linear regression works better when the variables we use in our model are not skewed (though they don’t have to necessarily be normally distributed). Because of this, we are going to see if square footage shares a linear relationship with house price when looking at the natural log-transformation (i.e. log() in R) of both variables. Keeping this in mind, create two new variables that represent the log-transformation of house price and square footage and add them to the dataset. Call these variables log_price and log_sqft respectively.


housing <- housing |>
  mutate(
    log_price = log(price),
    log_sqft = log(sqft)
  )

all.equal(housing, hw4_sol[["housing_p1d"]])

[1] TRUE

title: Homework 4 - STAT 1080
text:
Part e (3 points)
Now, use the log-transformed variables to make a scatterplot that relates the log-transformed square footage to the log-transformed prices. Do not distinguish the points by neighborhood in this plot. Use the same format and style considerations outlined in Part b to get your version of this plot to match the solution plot exactly.


ggplot(housing) +
  geom_point(aes(x = log_sqft, y = log_price)) +
  scale_x_continuous("Square Footage (log-scale)", limits = c(6.6, 9)) +
  scale_y_continuous("Price (log-scale)", limits = c(4.75, 8)) +
  theme_no_legend




Scatterplot relating square footage to house price.

title: Homework 4 - STAT 1080
text:
Part f (2 points)
Based on this plot, do you think it is appropriate to try and create a linear model that uses square footage to predict house price? Explain why or why not.


Answer: I would say that the data do seem to share a linear relationship (i.e. we could fit a straight line through the center of the points). Because of this, it seems appropriate to use linear regression to relate square footage and house price.

title: Homework 4 - STAT 1080
text:
Part g (3 points)
Using a similar plot style to Part e and an identical color scheme to Part f, plot the points using color to distinguish subdivisions. Use the geom_smooth(method = "lm") argument to look at estimated regression lines for each neighborhood.


ggplot(housing, aes(x = log_sqft, y = log_price, color = subdivision)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm") +
  scale_x_continuous("Square Footage (log-scale)", limits = c(6.6, 9)) +
  scale_y_continuous("Price (log-scale)", limits = c(4.75, 8)) +
  scale_color_brewer(type = "qual", palette = "Dark2") +
  theme_legend_left




Scatterplot relating square footage to house price by subdivision.

title: Homework 4 - STAT 1080
text:
Part h (3 points)
Based on those regression line and their associated confidence intervals (i.e., the gray shaded regions), does it visually appear at the relationship between house price and square footage is the same across all subdivisions? Explain why or why not (using visuals only, no statistical tests at this point).


Answer: The relationship appears to be identical for the Dunes West and Park West subdivisions, but very different for the Carolina Park Subdivision. Carolina Park house prices seem to be less responsive to changes in square footage than the other two neighborhoods.

title: Homework 4 - STAT 1080
text:
Part a (2 points)
Use the housing dataset that removed the missing price and square footage values and includes the log-transformed price and square footage variables. Create a simple linear regression model using the lm() function that uses the log-transformed square footage to predict the log-transformed price.


simple_lm <- lm(log_price ~ log_sqft, data = housing)

all.equal(simple_lm, hw4_sol[["p2a"]])

[1] TRUE

title: Homework 4 - STAT 1080
text:
Part b (3 points)
Use the predict() function with your newly created linear model to predict house prices from 1000 sqft to 3000 sqft in increments of 100. Remember that your predictions will be on the log scale, so you will need to use the exp() function to transform your predictions back to the original scale.


# The prediction data is provided. You just need to
# figure out how to obtain the predictions.
test_data <- data.frame(log_sqft = log(seq(1000, 3000, 100)))

# Get predictions
y_est <- predict(simple_lm, newdata = test_data)

# Exponentiate predictions
y_final <- exp(y_est)

all.equal(unname(y_final), hw4_sol[["y_est"]])

[1] TRUE

title: Homework 4 - STAT 1080
text:
Part c (2 points)
Lets now consider a model that includes both square footage and lot size (i.e. acres) as predictors. To do this, we will first need to create a log-transformed version of acres, i.e. log(acres + 0.1). The + 0.1 accommodates the fact that some of the homes have no lot since they are condos, and you cannot take the log of zero.
Add log_acres to your housing dataset and make sure that the new dataset matches the solution exactly.


housing <- housing |>
  mutate(log_acres = log(acres + 0.1))

all.equal(housing, hw4_sol[["housing_p2c"]])

[1] TRUE

title: Homework 4 - STAT 1080
text:
Part d (3 points)
Use the lm() function to create a linear model that uses log_acres and log_sqft to predict log_price. Confirm that your linear model matches the solution exactly.


test_lm_1 <- lm(log_price ~ log_sqft + log_acres, data = housing)

all.equal(test_lm_1, hw4_sol[["test_lm_1"]])

[1] TRUE

title: Homework 4 - STAT 1080
text:
Part e (5 points)
Use the confint() function to obtain 95% confidence intervals for all of the model coefficients. We wish to use the confidence intervals to determine if, after accounting for the square footage of the home, lot size is still significantly related to house price. Based on your confidence intervals, what do you conclude and why?


confint(test_lm_1)

                 2.5 %    97.5 %
(Intercept) -1.0974973 0.2632592
log_sqft     0.7950553 0.9580906
log_acres    0.1610430 0.2483307



Answer: There is significant evidence to suggest that, after accounting for home square footage, that lot size is linearly related to house price. We can say this because the chance that there is no relationship (i.e. a coefficient the log_acres term equal to 0) is very small based on our sample because our confidence interval does not include zero.

title: Homework 4 - STAT 1080
text:
Part a (5 points)
Use the tidy() function from the broom package to create a dataframe of coefficients (with associated confidence intervals) for three linear models, one for each subdivision, that use log_sqft and log_acres to predict log_price. Remember to use a group_by() operation on an appropriate variable in order to get the tidy() function to give you coefficients for three models instead of one.


# In order to match the solution, put log_sqft in your equation BEFORE
# log_acres.
lm_summary <- housing |>
  group_by(subdivision) |>
  reframe(tidy(lm(log_price ~ log_sqft + log_acres), conf.int = TRUE))

all.equal(lm_summary, hw4_sol[["lm_summary"]])

[1] TRUE

title: Homework 4 - STAT 1080
text:
Part b (5 points)
Use geom_segment() and facet_wrap() to plot the confidence intervals for the coefficients associated with log_sqft and log_acres. Most of the code is provided, but you need to figure out how to complete the statement for the geom_segment() function. Please consult the function documentation to do this. The result of this code is separate plots for the two variables, with subdivisions provided on the y-axis and the confidence intervals plotted on the x-axis (see the solution plot).


lm_summary |>
  filter(term != "(Intercept)") |> # don't plot the intercept coefficient
  ggplot() +
  geom_segment(aes(
    x = conf.low, xend = conf.high,
    y = subdivision, yend = subdivision
  ), lwd = 2) +
  facet_wrap(~term, scales = "free_x") +
  xlab("Coefficient Estimate") +
  ylab("Subdivision") +
  theme_no_legend




Plots of the confidence intervals associated with the subdivision-specific linear model coefficient estimates.

title: Homework 4 - STAT 1080
text:
Part c (3 points)
Interpret the results of Part a and b in a few sentences. Do the estimated coefficients appear to be roughly similar to the overall model results? Does your conclusions regarding the statistical significance (or lack thereof) in Problem 2, Part e fail to hold in any of the subdivision-specific models?


Answer: Home prices in Carolina Park seem to be much less responsive to house size as compared to the other two subdivisions. I say this because there is literally no overlap in the confidence intervals associated with coefficient estimates for log_sqft. The other two subdivisions seem to be similar in all respects, and the coefficient estimates associated with lot size seem to be roughly similar (as evidenced by confidence interval overlap) in all subdivisions.

title: 1.6 Introduction to RStudio
text:
The File Editor (Top Left)


The logo on the script file indicates the file type.
When an R file is open, there are Run and Source buttons on the top which allow you to run selected lines of code (Run) or source (run) the entire file.
Code line numbers are provided on the left (this is a handy way to see where in the code the errors occur), and you can see line:character numbers at the bottom left.
At the bottom right, there is another indicator of what type of file Rstudio thinks this is.

title: 1.6 Introduction to RStudio
text:
The File Editor (Top Left)


The logo on the script file indicates the file type.
When a quarto markdown file is open, there is a render button at the top which allows you to compile the file to see its “pretty”, non-markup form.
In the same toolbar, there are buttons to add a code chunk as well as to run a selcted line of code or chunk of code.
You can toggle between source (shown) and visual mode to see a more word-like rendering of the quarto markdown file.
Code line numbers are provided on the left (this is a handy way to see where in the code the errors occur), and you can see line:character numbers at the bottom left.
At the bottom right, there is another indicator of what type of file Rstudio thinks this is.

title: 1.6 Introduction to RStudio
text:
The File Editor (Top Left)


The logo on the text file indicates the file type.
When a text file (or other unknown file extension) is open, there are very few buttons in the editor window.
Code line numbers are provided on the left (this is a handy way to see where in the code the errors occur), and you can see line:character numbers at the bottom left.
At the bottom right, there is another indicator of what type of file Rstudio thinks this is.

title: 1.6 Introduction to RStudio
text:
The Console Pane (Bottom Left)


When running R code from a script file, the console will show you that you are running in R by the logo at the top of the console pane.
You will initially see lines indicating that you’re running R (they’re missing here because this isn’t the first command I ran in this session).
The command you ran will appear after >, and the results will appear immediately below, with boxed numbers in front of each sequential line.
A > waits for a new command.
In the environment pane, you may see a new value pop up named .Last.value - this is part of user settings and you can stop it from appearing if you want to.

title: 1.6 Introduction to RStudio
text:
Environment Tab (Top Right)


The environment tab shows you all of the objects in memory that the language you’re working in knows about.

title: 1.6 Introduction to RStudio
text:
History Tab (Top Right)


The history tab shows you a list of all commands you’ve run and allows you to send them to the console or to source (the text editor).

title: 1.6 Introduction to RStudio
text:
Files Tab (Bottom Right)


The files tab shows you the files in your current working directory (by default), though you can navigate through it and find other files as necessary.
If you want to return to your working directory, there’s a button for that in the “More” menu.
One of the most important pieces of information in this pane is your path - you can construct the file path by using ~/ for home, and then for each folder, adding a slash between. The path to the folder we’re looking at here is thus ~/Projects/Class/stat-computing-r-python/.

title: 1.6 Introduction to RStudio
text:
Packages Tab (Bottom Right)


You can get important information from the packages tab, like what packages are loaded, easy access to documentation for each package, and what version of the package is installed.

title: 1.6 Introduction to RStudio
text:
Help tab (Bottom Right)


The help tab makes it easy to get access to function documentation within Rstudio, so you don’t have to switch windows.

title: 1.6 Introduction to RStudio
text:
The Viewer Tab (Bottom Right)


The Viewer tab is where you will preview quarto documents – which is how you will submit some labs and homework assignments in this class.
You should always preview your documents before submitting them to make sure they look correct.
You can also set a specific quarto document to open in a browser or in the system PDF viewer.

text:
Simpson’s Paradox






NoteDefinition: Simpson’s Paradox



A phenomenon in which a trend appears in several groups of data but disappears or reverses when groups are combined


Arises from

confounding variables
clustered data
failure to manage causal data
extremely different rates or amounts of data across categories

title: 1.8 Bias and Ethics
text:
Simpson’s Paradox, Visually






Negative association between x and y







Positive association between x and y, within each group







???







When interpreting results, it’s critical to explain both the group-wise trend and the overall trend.
This can get complicated
Data ethics means explaining things in context and not stopping at the first plot or model
Even if the first plot or model matches your expectations

title: 1.8 Bias and Ethics
text:
Ethics


Understand how the data was collected

potential biases
missing observations

Understand relationships between variables

including variables that may not be present in the data

Interpret results with humility

allow for the possibility that you don’t have all the information
consider how data, model, or interpretation might be wrong

As a consumer, be skeptical, especially when results confirm your prior beliefs

text:
Statistics
Sometimes, we want to compute statistics based on our data, and map geoms to those computations.


Smooth or Trend Line: stat_smooth()


geom_line(aes(x = after_stat(x),     
              y = after_stat(y))) +    
geom_ribbon(    
  aes(x = after_stat(x), 
      ymin = after_stat(ymin), 
      ymax = after_stat(ymax)))


Boxplots (5-number summary): stat_boxplot()


geom_boxplot() 
# A shortcut for something like this:
geom_rect(aes(xmin = x - after_stat(width)/2,
              xmax = x + after_stat(width)/2,
              ymin = after_stat(lower),
              ymax = after_stat(upper)) + 
geom_segment(aes(x = x - after_stat(width)/2,
                 xend = x + after_stat(width)/2,
                 y = after_stat(middle),
                 yend = after_stat(middle))) + 
geom_segment(aes(x = x, xend = xend, 
                 y = after_stat(lower),
                 yend = after_stat(ymin))) + 
geom_segment(aes(x = x, xend = xend, 
                 y = after_stat(upper),
                 yend = after_stat(ymax)))

Statistics
Sometimes, we want to compute statistics based on our data, and map geoms to those computations.


bar plots (count up data by category): stat_count()


geom_bar(aes(x = x, y = after_stat(count)))
# A shortcut for something like this:
geom_rect(aes(xmin = x - after_stat(width),
              xmax = x + after_stat(width),
              ymin = 0,
              ymax = after_stat(count)))


Histograms (cut into bins, then count): stat_bin()


geom_histogram(aes(x = x, y = after_stat(count)))
# A shortcut for something like this:
geom_rect(aes(xmin = after_stat(xstart),
              xmax = after_stat(xend),
              ymin = 0,
              ymax = after_stat(count)))


Frequency Polygons (cut into bins, then count): stat_bin()


geom_freqpoly(aes(x = x, y = after_stat(count)))
# A shortcut for something like this:
geom_line(aes(x = x,
              y = after_stat(count)))

                 xend = x_prev,

                 yend = after_stat(prop))) +
